messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sione, an American of Samoan descent, was thirty-two when the timber scaffolding gave way without warning at his brother’s renovation site. He had been passing up a steel bracket, only to watch the platform snap and his brother plummet into the open excavation below. There was a sickening impact, then the terrifying sight of his brother’s hands curled inward and the exact red stain spreading across his shirt. Sione dropped to his knees, his own limbs locked, certain he should have shouted or caught him before the fall. His brother did not survive the night, and the collapse left Sione with a haunting understanding of why certain images would later pierce his composure. In the months that followed, his inability to articulate the event became the gateway to his recurring distress. His conviction that he is a weak person and that he failed to protect his brother does not stay contained to his thoughts; it actively shapes how his mind retrieves the past. Because he believes he is a helpless object, his memories refuse to form into coherent narratives. Instead, when he tries to explain what happened to anyone, he loses the thread and cannot finish, leaving the silence heavy and unbroken. The moment he stops speaking, the auditory recall of splintering wood and his brother’s final exhale floods his skull, accompanied by overwhelming grief that leaves him gasping on the floor. His self-appraisals of dehumanization and failure dictate what pulls him out of the present and into that paralyzing loop. He is certain that his own numbness makes him dangerous, so the sight of specific body parts immediately activates a visceral alarm. Since his divorce, Sione has clung to the structured routine of childcare, but the suburban home with its steep wooden staircase and sunlit backyard patio has become a minefield of conditioned dread. When he noticed a toddler trip on the rug and scrape his knee, his eyes locked onto the specific abrasion on the child’s shin before darting away as his chest tightened. The visual cue, the reminders of victims that surface during his weekly support calls, and the loss themes that arise when others talk about people losing loved ones do not merely remind him of the past; they confirm his belief that he is merely an object watching life pass him by, forcing him to hover over the children with rigid avoidance. Yet, it is the memories themselves that ultimately cement his darkest convictions. Each time the auditory echoes return or the grief on recall floods his system, he is forced to confront the narrative he cannot complete. The very act of losing the thread in his explanation proves his weakness to him, and the paralyzing grief that follows reinforces his certainty that he should have protected others. Over the years, this loop has hardened into a quiet exhaustion. Sione has stopped attending family dinners, avoids parents who discuss accidents, and flinches when the family’s older dog runs too fast across the patio. It was the mother’s aide who finally noticed his distracted gaze and the way he froze when a child cried out during play, which is what finally brought him to this intake. He is terrified that he is so hollowed out he cannot truly care for another child, and what he hopes for is simply a way to remember without losing himself.
